title: Python for AI
blurb: Enough Python, NumPy and pandas to read and run every code example in the later courses.

lessons.title: Set up: notebooks in Google Colab
lessons.summary: Run Python in the browser with nothing to install.
body: A **notebook** is a document that mixes code, its results and your notes in one place. Instead of one long program, you write small **cells** and run them one at a time, seeing each result right underneath. It is like a lab notebook where every experiment shows its outcome next to it.

**Google Colab** gives you free notebooks that run in your browser on Google's computers. All you need is a Google account: go to colab.research.google.com, click New notebook, type `print("hello")` in a cell and press Shift+Enter. Popular AI libraries like NumPy, pandas and scikit-learn are already installed.

Notebooks remember what you have run. A variable created in one cell can be used in any later cell, but only after you have run the cell that creates it. If things get confusing, use **Runtime > Restart and run all** to start fresh from the top.

Colab also has **text cells** for notes and a free GPU option for heavier deep learning later on. Your notebooks save to Google Drive, so you can come back to them or share them like any other document.
keyIdeas: A notebook is made of cells you run one at a time.
Colab runs Python in your browser with nothing to install.
Variables carry over between cells once you run them.
Restart and run all is the fix when the notebook gets muddled.

quiz.q: What happens when you run a notebook cell?
options: The code runs and its output appears below it
quiz.explain: Each cell's output appears right under it, which makes experimenting easy.

quiz.q: You get NameError for a variable defined in an earlier cell. What is the likely cause?
options: That earlier cell has not been run yet
quiz.explain: A variable exists only after the cell that creates it has been run in this session.

code.title: first_cells.py
code.source:
# A notebook is a list of cells. Each cell is a small piece of code you run
# on its own, and the result appears right underneath it.

# Cell 1: Python works like a calculator.
print(2 + 3 * 4)

# Cell 2: variables you create stay around for later cells.
name = "Ada"
hours_per_week = 3

# Cell 3: use them again.
weeks = 8
print(f"{name} will study for {hours_per_week * weeks} hours in {weeks} weeks.")

# Cell 4: check which Python version is running.
import sys
print("Python version:", sys.version.split()[0])
code.note: Each comment block is like one notebook cell; in Colab you would run them one by one.

lessons.title: Python basics
lessons.summary: Variables, types, functions, conditions, loops, lists and dicts.
body: A **variable** is a labeled box that holds a value: `city = "Lisbon"`. The main basic **types** are text (`str`), whole numbers (`int`), decimals (`float`) and `True`/`False` values (`bool`). Python works out the type for you.

A **function** is a reusable recipe. You define it once with `def`, give it inputs, and it `return`s a result. Inside, **conditions** (`if`, `elif`, `else`) let your code make choices, like picking "hot" or "cold" based on the temperature.

A **list** keeps items in order, like a shopping list: `[18.0, 26.5, 12.0]`. A `for` **loop** goes through the items one by one so you can do the same thing to each. Python uses indentation (spaces at the start of a line) to show which lines belong inside a loop, function or `if`.

A **dict** (dictionary) stores pairs of keys and values, so you can look things up by name: `capitals["France"]` gives `"Paris"`. Lists and dicts are everywhere in AI code, for example a list of training examples or a dict of settings.
keyIdeas: Variables hold values; common types are str, int, float and bool.
Functions are reusable recipes; if/elif/else make decisions.
Lists hold ordered items and for loops walk through them.
Dicts map keys to values for quick lookup.

quiz.q: What is the type of the value 21.5?
quiz.explain: Numbers with a decimal point are floats.

quiz.q: How would you get Tokyo from capitals = {"Japan": "Tokyo"}?
quiz.explain: You look up a dict value by its key, here "Japan".

code.title: basics.py
code.source:
# Variables and types
city = "Lisbon"          # str (text)
temperature = 21.5       # float (decimal number)
days = 3                 # int (whole number)
is_sunny = True          # bool (True or False)

# A function: a reusable recipe with inputs and an output
def describe(temp):
    if temp >= 25:
        return "hot"
    elif temp >= 15:
        return "mild"
    else:
        return "cold"

print(city, "is", describe(temperature))

# A list: an ordered collection
forecast = [18.0, 26.5, 12.0]
for day, temp in enumerate(forecast, start=1):
    print(f"Day {day}: {temp} degrees, {describe(temp)}")

# A dict: look up values by a key, like a real dictionary
capitals = {"France": "Paris", "Japan": "Tokyo"}
capitals["Peru"] = "Lima"
for country, capital in capitals.items():
    print(f"The capital of {country} is {capital}")
print("Number of countries:", len(capitals))
code.note: Change the numbers and names, run it again, and see what changes.

lessons.title: Going further: the official tutorial
lessons.summary: Data structures, modules and errors, as reference reading.
body: The official Python tutorial is the best free reference, and you do not need to read it all at once. Treat it like a cookbook: dip in when you need a recipe. The sections on data structures, modules and errors are the most useful for AI work.

Beyond lists and dicts, Python has **tuples** (like lists but fixed, written with round brackets) and **sets** (collections with no duplicates). A **list comprehension** builds a new list in one line, such as `[n * n for n in numbers]`, and you will see them constantly in AI code.

A **module** is a file of ready-made code you bring in with `import`. Python ships with many, like `math`, `random` and `collections`. Libraries such as NumPy and pandas are just bigger modules installed separately.

When something goes wrong, Python raises an **exception** with a message and a traceback. Read it from the bottom up: the last line says what went wrong. With `try` and `except` you can catch an expected error and handle it calmly instead of letting the program crash.
keyIdeas: Use the official tutorial as a reference, not a cover-to-cover read.
Tuples are fixed lists; sets remove duplicates; comprehensions build lists fast.
import brings in modules of ready-made code.
Read errors from the bottom line up; try/except handles expected ones.

quiz.q: What does [n * 2 for n in [1, 2, 3]] produce?
quiz.explain: A list comprehension applies n * 2 to every item, giving [2, 4, 6].

quiz.q: Where in a Python traceback do you find what actually went wrong?
quiz.explain: The last line names the error type and message.

code.title: beyond_basics.py
code.source:
import math                      # a module: ready-made code you import
from collections import Counter  # import one tool from a module

# List comprehension: build a new list in one line
numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
squares = [n * n for n in numbers if n % 2 == 0]
print("Even squares:", squares)

# Tuples and sets
point = (3, 4)                   # tuple: fixed, cannot be changed
print("Distance from origin:", math.hypot(*point))
tags = {"ai", "python", "ai"}    # set: duplicates disappear
print("Unique tags:", sorted(tags))

# Counting things with a module
words = "the cat and the hat and the bat".split()
print("Most common:", Counter(words).most_common(2))

# Errors: handle them instead of crashing
def safe_divide(a, b):
    try:
        return a / b
    except ZeroDivisionError:
        print("Cannot divide by zero, returning None")
        return None

print(safe_divide(10, 4))
print(safe_divide(1, 0))
code.note: Use this as a sampler, then read the matching sections of the official tutorial.

lessons.title: NumPy: arrays and fast math
lessons.summary: Arrays, shapes, indexing, broadcasting and aggregations.

resources.title: NumPy: the absolute basics for beginners

body: **NumPy** is the foundation of almost all AI code in Python. Its core object is the **array**: a grid of numbers of the same type. A 1D array is a row of numbers, a 2D array is a table, and higher dimensions hold things like images and batches of data.

Every array has a **shape**, written as a tuple like `(2, 3)` meaning 2 rows and 3 columns. Checking `.shape` is the single most useful debugging habit in AI work, because most bugs are shapes that do not line up.

You pick out values with **indexing** and **slicing**: `scores[1, 2]` is row 1, column 2 (counting from 0), and `scores[:, 0]` is the whole first column. A **boolean mask** like `scores[scores > 80]` keeps only the values that match a condition.

Math on arrays works on every element at once, with no loop needed, and it is much faster than plain Python. **Broadcasting** stretches a smaller array to fit a bigger one, so multiplying a table by a row of three weights applies each weight to its column. **Aggregations** like `.mean()`, `.sum()` and `.max()` can work on the whole array or along an `axis`.
keyIdeas: Arrays are fast grids of numbers; NumPy powers most AI libraries.
Always check .shape; mismatched shapes cause most bugs.
Index with [row, col], slice with :, filter with boolean masks.
Math is element-wise, broadcasting stretches shapes, axis picks direction.

quiz.q: An array has shape (2, 3). What does that mean?
quiz.explain: Shape lists the size of each dimension: rows first, then columns.

quiz.q: For a 2D array, what does .mean(axis=1) give you?
options: One average for the whole array
quiz.explain: axis=1 averages across the columns, giving one value per row.

code.title: arrays.py
code.source:
import numpy as np

# An array holds many numbers of the same type
scores = np.array([[90, 75, 60],     # each row: one student
                   [80, 85, 95]])    # each column: one test
print("Shape (rows, columns):", scores.shape)

# Indexing and slicing
print("Student 2, test 3:", scores[1, 2])
print("All of test 1:", scores[:, 0])

# Math on the whole array at once (no loops!)
print("Plus 5 bonus points:\n", scores + 5)

# Broadcasting: a small array is stretched to match a bigger one
weights = np.array([0.2, 0.3, 0.5])  # one weight per test
print("Weighted scores:\n", scores * weights)

# Aggregations, along a chosen axis
print("Average per student:", scores.mean(axis=1).round(1))
print("Best per test:", scores.max(axis=0))

# Boolean masks: pick values that match a condition
print("Scores above 80:", scores[scores > 80])

lessons.title: pandas: working with tables
lessons.summary: DataFrames: select, filter, group and read CSV files.
body: **pandas** is the go-to tool for table data in Python, like a spreadsheet you control with code. A table is called a **DataFrame**: rows of records and named columns. A single column is a **Series**.

Most data arrives as a CSV file, and `pd.read_csv("file.csv")` loads it in one line. Then take a first look with `df.head()` for the first rows, `df.shape` for the size, and `df.describe()` for quick statistics.

Select a column with `df["hours"]`, and several with `df[["name", "hours"]]`. **Filter** rows with a condition inside the brackets, like `df[df["hours"] > 5]`. Create a new column just by assigning to it, and pandas does the math for every row at once.

**Grouping** answers questions like "what is the total per team?": `df.groupby("team")["hours"].sum()`. Together with `sort_values`, these few moves cover most of the data preparation you will do before training a model.
keyIdeas: A DataFrame is a table; each column is a Series.
read_csv loads data; head, shape and describe give a first look.
Filter rows with df[condition]; select columns by name.
groupby plus sum or mean summarizes data by category.

quiz.q: How do you keep only the rows where hours is above 5?
quiz.explain: Putting a True/False condition inside the brackets keeps the matching rows.

quiz.q: Which pandas method would give total sales per region?
quiz.explain: groupby splits rows by region so you can sum each group.

code.title: tables.py
code.source:
import io
import pandas as pd

# Pretend this text is a CSV file on disk
csv_text = """name,team,hours,tasks
Ana,red,5,3
Ben,blue,8,6
Cara,red,3,2
Dev,blue,6,5
Eli,red,7,6"""
df = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(csv_text))  # normally: pd.read_csv("file.csv")

print(df.head(), "\n")
print("Columns:", list(df.columns), "| rows:", len(df), "\n")

# Select a column, and add a new one
df["tasks_per_hour"] = (df["tasks"] / df["hours"]).round(2)

# Filter rows with a condition
print("Worked more than 5 hours:")
print(df[df["hours"] > 5][["name", "hours"]], "\n")

# Group and summarize
print("Totals by team:")
print(df.groupby("team")[["hours", "tasks"]].sum(), "\n")

# Sort
print(df.sort_values("tasks_per_hour", ascending=False).head(3))
code.note: io.StringIO lets the CSV text act like a file; with a real file just pass its name.

lessons.title: Plotting your data
lessons.summary: Line, bar and scatter plots with Matplotlib and Seaborn.
body: A chart often shows in a second what a table hides: a trend, an outlier, a pattern. **Matplotlib** is Python's main plotting library, and **Seaborn** is built on top of it to make good-looking statistical charts with less code.

Pick the chart by the question. A **line plot** shows how something changes over time. A **bar chart** compares amounts across categories. A **scatter plot** puts two numbers against each other to show whether they move together.

The basic Matplotlib pattern is: create a figure and axes with `plt.subplots()`, draw on the axes with `.plot()`, `.bar()` or `.scatter()`, add a title and axis labels, then `plt.show()`. With pandas you can also call `df.plot()` directly on a table.

In AI work you will plot constantly: looking at your data before modelling, and drawing **training curves** to see if a model is still improving. Always label your axes; a chart nobody can read is a chart nobody uses.
keyIdeas: Line for change over time, bar for comparing categories, scatter for relationships.
Pattern: fig, ax = plt.subplots(), draw, label, plt.show().
Seaborn builds on Matplotlib for nicer statistical charts.
Always label axes and titles.

quiz.q: Which chart best shows whether study hours relate to test scores?
quiz.explain: A scatter plot shows how two numeric values move together.

quiz.q: Which chart fits monthly website visits over a year?
quiz.explain: Line plots are made for showing change over time.

code.title: three_plots.py
code.source:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

months = ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun"]
sales = [12, 15, 14, 20, 24, 27]

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
ad_spend = rng.uniform(1, 10, 40)
visits = 30 * ad_spend + rng.normal(0, 25, 40)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.5))

# Line plot: how something changes over time
axes[0].plot(months, sales, marker="o")
axes[0].set_title("Line: sales over time")

# Bar plot: compare categories
axes[1].bar(["A", "B", "C"], [40, 25, 35], color="tab:orange")
axes[1].set_title("Bar: sales by product")

# Scatter plot: is there a relationship between two numbers?
axes[2].scatter(ad_spend, visits, alpha=0.7)
axes[2].set_xlabel("Ad spend")
axes[2].set_ylabel("Visits")
axes[2].set_title("Scatter: spend vs visits")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
code.note: The site draws the open figure as an image under the output.
